title: Long Mott (Dow / X-energy): 2026/10/07 - Comment (5) E-mail regarding LMGS CP Hearing [['General FR Notice Comment Letter']]

documents.text:
From:                   Dan Lê <dan@sanantoniobaywaterkeeper.org>
Sent:                   Wednesday, October 7, 2026 12:36 AM
To:                     LMGS-CPHearing Resource
Subject:                [External_Sender] Written comments – Docket ID NRC-2025-0079 (Docket
                        No. 50-614)

Re: Long Mott Generating Station construction permit, Docket ID NRC-2025-0079 (Docket
No. 50-614)

Dear NRC Staff:

My name is Dan Le, staff member of San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper. I asked
several of these questions orally at the September 22, 2026 hearing. These written
comments supplement those questions. Under the Commission's June 2026 Policy
Statement on Mandatory Hearings (91 FR 34661), I request that every question below
receive a written response in the meeting summary addendum.

Several oral answers given by NRC staff at the hearing appear inconsistent with the
applicant's own Preliminary Safety Analysis Report, Revision 1 (ML26261A423). I identify
each inconsistency below and respectfully ask NRC staff to correct or explain it in writing.

There are a number of issues I believe should be addressed at the construction permit
stage. Staff noted at the hearing that a construction permit does not authorize operation
and that further analysis will follow at the operating license stage. Under 10 CFR 50.35(a),
however, design information may be deferred to the final safety analysis report only if it
"can reasonably be left for later consideration." Two of the issues below do not meet that
standard:

   •   Flood protection is fixed by construction. The PSAR's primary flood protection
       mechanism is locating safety-related equipment above the design flood level. Floor
       elevations, below-grade structures, and the spent fuel storage building's 27.4 ft
       floor are set when concrete is poured, during construction, and cannot reasonably
       be revisited at the operating license stage. Section 50.35(a)(4)(ii) also requires a
       finding now, taking into consideration the Part 100 site criteria, that the facility can
       be constructed and operated at this location without undue risk. Those criteria
       include the site's hydrology (10 CFR 100.20(c) and 100.21(d)).
   •   The environmental review happens now. The environmental assessment is the
       agency's environmental review for this facility; the May 2026 notice states that at
       the operating license stage, staff will review the application for new and significant
       information. The EA defers site-specific flood protection to the safety review, and
       the safety review defers detailed flood protection to the operating license. As a
       result, the environmental consequences of a design-basis flood at this site,
       including at the spent fuel storage building, are not evaluated at either stage.
 I request that NRC staff state in writing whether detailed flood protection and the
environmental consequences of design-basis flooding can reasonably be left for later
consideration under 10 CFR 50.35(a), and if so, on what basis.

1. Flooding: staff's oral answer conflicts with PSAR Revision 1

In response to my question at the hearing, staff stated that safety-related components are
at a grade where they will not be impacted by flooding, and that staff had no flooding
concern because of a bluff that routes floodwater away from the site, with most flooding
occurring several miles away.

PSAR Revision 1 presents a more qualified picture:

   •   Table 2.0-1 lists site grade at 31 ft NAVD 88 and the Probable Maximum Storm Surge
       at 36.38 ft NAVD 88 still water, and 46.49 ft NAVD 88 with wave runup.
   •   Section 2.4.10 identifies maximum storm surge as the controlling flood event for the
       site, and adopts both levels as design basis hazard levels.
   •   The safety-related structure's finished floor is 31.5 ft NAVD 88. The PSAR states this
       "indicates that flood protection for safety-related SSCs is necessary."
   •   The bluff and the 1.65-mile buffer described in the PSAR apply to Guadalupe River
       flooding and upstream dam failure. They do not apply to Gulf storm surge.
   •   Section 2.4.10.3 adopts a preliminary strategy of locating safety-related SSCs
       above the 36.38 ft still-water level, with incorporated flood protection (flood-
       resistant construction, waterstops, penetration seals) for any that cannot be. The
       specific application, sizing, and configuration of those features will be developed
       for final design, and detailed flooding mitigation plans will be provided with the
       operating license application.


Questions:

   1. The controlling design-basis flood is storm surge at 36.38 ft NAVD 88, which PSAR
      Section 2.4.10.1 describes as "the elevation to which flood waters may rise and
      remain during the design basis flood event." That is roughly 5 ft above the safety-
      related structure's floor. Which safety-related SSCs sit below that level and will rely
      on incorporated barriers such as seals and waterstops rather than elevation? Given
      that their specific application, sizing, and configuration for individual systems will
      not be developed until final design, what is the basis for staff's oral statement that
      safety-related components will not be impacted?
   2. Did staff's statement about the bluff and water flowing away from the site refer to
      riverine and dam-failure flooding rather than storm surge? Please explain how the
      bluff affects the storm surge hazard, if at all.
    3. What specific flood protection features has staff relied on to find the site
      acceptable for a construction permit, given that detailed flood mitigation is deferred
      to the operating license application?
   4. What site layout, foundation, or structural decisions made during construction
      would constrain flood protection options later? How will staff ensure construction
      does not foreclose adequate protection? PSAR Section 2.4.10.4 states that plant
      final design related to elevations will use the design basis flood levels, and that any
      dedicated flood protection structure identified during detailed design, such as a
      floodwall, will be described in the FSAR with an evaluation of its effects on site
      hydraulics. Would the environmental effects of such a structure be evaluated under
      NEPA before it is built?
   5. What sea level rise assumption is included in the storm surge analysis in Revision 1,
      and over what plant lifetime?
   6. Will staff's site visit on September 22, 2026 and the flooding presentation staff
      received be documented in a publicly available trip report or meeting summary?


2. Revision 1 contains material changes; renewed request for more time

When I asked to extend the comment period, staff said Revision 1 contained nothing
materially significant. The applicant's own documents show changed safety conclusions:

   •   Basin embankment failure: 31.8 ft NAVD 88 in Rev. 0 (p. 2.4-50) vs. 32.5 ft in Rev. 1
       (p. 2.4-50).
   •   Basin failure conclusion: "indicates no flooding" in Rev. 0 vs. "flood protection for
       safety-related SSCs is necessary" in Rev. 1.
   •   Storm surge: 41.47 ft (SLOSH screening, with 10% uncertainty margin) in Rev. 0 vs.
       36.38 ft still water and 46.49 ft with wave runup in Rev. 1 (Table 2.0-1).

The March 2025 application also stated that the later site-specific results were not
expected to impact the maximum water level estimates. The design levels and at least one
safety conclusion did change: the storm surge still-water estimate went down, while the
basin-failure level went up and its conclusion reversed. Revision 1 is roughly 2,820 pages,
and the document file is dated September 18, 2026, four days before the hearing.

Questions and requests:

   1. On what basis did staff conclude that Revision 1 contains nothing materially
      significant, given the reversed basin-failure conclusion and the revised design flood
      levels?
   2. When was Revision 1 docketed and made publicly available in ADAMS?
   3. Does Revision 1 change any other safety conclusion, licensing basis event, or site
      characteristic from Revision 0? Please provide a list of changes, or identify where
      the applicant's change summary can be found.
    4. I again would like to request that the written comment period be extended by at
      least 30 days so the public can review Revision 1. If staff declines, please explain
      why.


3. The environmental assessment and finding of no significant impact

In response to my question at the hearing, staff stated that the flooding information
developed after the environmental assessment had no effect on it. Rather than address
the exemption question directly, staff described how the environmental assessment
pathway was selected when the application came in, and said staff would have reverted to
an EIS if it could not reach a finding of no significant impact for any resource area. Staff did
not explain the basis for exempting this application from the EIS requirement. The May 20,
2026 Federal Register notice (FR Doc. 2026-10073) grants one-time exemptions from 10
CFR 51.20(b)(1), 51.25, and 51.75(a), and rests its public-interest finding on the NRC's
efficiency principle.

Questions:

   1. The notice states that staff did not apply the 10 CFR 51.20 criteria and instead relied
      on "factors unique to" this application. What were those factors? Why do they
      justify departing, for a first-of-a-kind design at a hurricane-exposed coastal site,
      from a rule requiring an EIS for every power reactor construction permit?
   2. The EA's flooding discussion (Section 3.4, p. 3-13) relies on the FEMA flood map
      designation of Zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard, notes that no detailed flood
      hazard study has been conducted for West Coloma Creek (although PSAR Table
      2.0-1 lists a maximum still-water flood elevation of 32 ft NAVD 88 for the creek,
      above the 31.5 ft safety-related floors), and states that site-specific flood protection
      is considered in the safety review. The PSAR, however, sets a design-basis storm
      surge about 5 ft above the safety-related floors and defers detailed flood protection
      to the operating license application. How does staff reconcile the EA's
      characterization of minimal flood hazard with that design-basis flood? At the
      construction permit stage, where are the environmental consequences of a design-
      basis storm surge at this site, including releases of radiological or hazardous
      materials, evaluated? Explain the basis for the oral statement that the revised flood
      conclusions had no effect on the EA.
   3. The notice says the decision to prepare an EA followed staff's initial review of the
      applicant's Environmental Report. When was that decision made, and is it
      documented? Which resource areas had staff not yet independently evaluated at
      that time?
   4. When were the Endangered Species Act and Essential Fish Habitat consultations
      with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service
      completed, relative to the May 2026 FONSI? Please provide ADAMS accession
       numbers for the biological assessment, any essential fish habitat assessment, and
      agency responses.
   5. The EA (Section 3.15.1.1) relies on design basis accident doses LME provided in a
      November 6, 2025 RAI response, scaled using ratios from PSAR Section 2.3.4.3.
      Revision 1 now asks that Section 2.3.4.3's dispersion methodology be withheld as
      proprietary. Can the public review the dispersion values underlying the EA's
      accident conclusions, and were any of them changed in Revision 1? If site-specific
      meteorological data later produces less favorable dispersion, will the EA be
      supplemented?
   6. How did the EA account for cumulative impacts in a watershed and airshed that
      already includes the Dow Seadrift complex, Formosa Plastics, Alcoa, the Lavaca
      Bay mercury Superfund site, ongoing plastic pellet discharges now subject to
      litigation, and pending wastewater permit renewals?
   7. The EA (Section 3.4.3) reports average withdrawals of 9.92 cfs and average
      consumptive use of 6.3 cfs from the Calhoun Canal under Dow's existing water
      rights. Because records of the existing co-generation station's water use are not
      available, the EA instead adds projected LMGS use to a single year (2022) of Dow
      withdrawal data, and compares withdrawals to mean monthly Guadalupe River
      flows from 2000 to 2023 (p. 3-15). What share of river flow would maximum
      withdrawals represent during the lowest-flow months on record, including drought
      years, when freshwater inflows to San Antonio Bay matter most? And why is a single
      year of withdrawal data an adequate baseline?
   8. The EA (Section 3.16, p. 3-68) acknowledges that hurricane storm surges will tend
      to be more severe because of higher relative sea levels and possibly more intense
      hurricanes. Its conclusion that impacts would not be materially altered relies on the
      site not being within a designated floodplain and on NRC safety requirements that
      structures important to safety withstand flooding and sea level rise (p. 3-69). Since
      detailed flood protection is deferred to the operating license and the spent fuel
      storage building is not safety-related, what analysis supports that conclusion at the
      construction permit stage?
   9. The notice says staff will review any operating license application for new and
      significant information. Will that review specifically cover site-specific meteorology,
      final flood protection, and the final emergency planning zone analysis? Will staff
      prepare an EIS if those differ materially from the EA's assumptions?


4. Emergency planning and functional containment

In response to my questions at the hearing, staff confirmed that the Xe-100 has no
pressure-retaining containment and relies on "functional containment" provided by the
TRISO fuel. Staff also confirmed that the plume exposure emergency planning zone is
currently set at the site boundary, about 400 meters, subject to confirmation at the
operating license stage. PSAR Revision 1, Section 11.4.5, states that "pre-planned offsite
protective actions are not required." The supporting analysis is preliminary and uses
 generic dispersion factors. Revision 1 says a representative analysis using nearby airport
data will come in a later PSAR revision, and data from the on-site meteorological tower, not
yet in service, will come with the operating license application (Sections 2.3.2.1.1 and
11.4).

Staff also confirmed that the design, in its entirety, has not been tested.

Questions:

   1. When will the on-site meteorological tower be placed in service, and how many
      years of on-site data will be required before the emergency planning zone analysis
      is finalized?
   2. What criteria will staff apply at the operating license stage to decide whether the
      zone must be expanded beyond the site boundary? If it is expanded, what offsite
      planning would then be required for Seadrift and Port Lavaca?
   3. Is any NRC finding about the emergency planning zone being made at the
      construction permit stage? If so, is it binding at the operating license stage, or will it
      be reviewed from scratch?
   4. Because functional containment depends on fuel performance, what fuel failure
      fraction is assumed in the bounding dose analyses supporting the site-boundary
      zone? What irradiation and post-irradiation test data support that assumption?
   5. Will the Calhoun County and Victoria County emergency management offices, local
      hospitals, and Seadrift residents be consulted before the zone is finalized?
   6. 10 CFR 100.21(c) requires that site atmospheric dispersion characteristics be
      evaluated and dispersion parameters established as a site criterion, and 10 CFR
      100.20(c)(2) requires that meteorological characteristics necessary for the safety
      analysis be identified and characterized. How do generic dispersion factors and off-
      site airport data satisfy these requirements at the construction permit stage, before
      any on-site meteorological data exist?
   7. 10 CFR 100.21(g) requires identification of physical characteristics unique to the
      site that could significantly impede the development of emergency plans. Has
      hurricane storm surge, flooding of evacuation routes from Seadrift and Port Lavaca,
      and the site's location within an operating chemical complex been evaluated as
      potential impediments? Where is that evaluation documented?


5. Water use, liquid effluents, and backup cooling

In answer to a resident's question about well water, staff said the design has no effluent
and, because it does not operate with water, there is no concern about water released
from the plant. PSAR Revision 1 describes otherwise:

   •   A Liquid Radioactive Waste Handling System (Figure 9.2-1) and a liquid radwaste
       inventory in the Radwaste Building (Table 3.10-5).
    •   Section 2.4.13, "Accidental Releases of Liquid Effluents into Ground and Surface
       Waters."
   •   A water-filled Reactor Cavity Cooling System. In its passive boil-off mode, four
       makeup supply tanks per module provide gravity-fed cooling for 72 hours (Sections
       1.1.4 and 6.4.11).

Staff also said that cooldown after an event takes days to weeks.

Questions:

   1. Please correct or clarify the statement that the plant has no effluent. What liquid
      radioactive wastes will be generated, how will they be stored and disposed of, and
      what are the pathways to groundwater and surface water analyzed in Section
      2.4.13?
   2. What conclusions does Section 2.4.13 reach about an accidental release reaching
      drinking water wells in the Seadrift and Port Lavaca areas or the Victoria Barge
      Canal?
   3. The passive boil-off mode provides 72 hours of cooling, but cooldown may take
      days to weeks. What is the source of makeup water after 72 hours if offsite power
      and the Dow site's water systems are unavailable, for example after a hurricane or
      an industrial accident at the Dow complex?
   4. Is the steam released in boil-off mode expected to carry any radioactivity under any
      licensing basis event?
   5. Staff's answer about the water supply for backup cooling was unclear. The EA
      reports that plant water comes from Dow's Basin #5, supplied from the Calhoun
      Canal. Is backup cooling makeup water drawn from the same source, and is any
      supply reserved for it?


6. Fuel testing, first-of-a-kind status, and applicant qualifications

Staff confirmed the design, in its entirety, has not been tested, yet also stated that
commercial deployment is not an experiment. The project is a DOE Advanced Reactor
Demonstration Program project. PSAR Revision 1 states that results of the applicant's
research and development program will be provided in the FSAR, with outstanding safety
questions to be resolved at or before completion of construction.

On qualifications, staff indicated that Long Mott Energy has partnered with X-energy and
another company to operate the facility, and described staff's review of whether the
applicant has adequate technical and financial qualifications. PSAR Revision 1 (Section
2.1.2) states that information about future agreements between Dow and the operator will
be provided in the operating license application.

Questions:
    1. Is the pebble fuel irradiated in the qualification campaign at the Advanced Test
      Reactor the same size, geometry, and manufacturing process as the fuel to be used
      at Long Mott? If not, how will staff confirm that test results apply to the production
      fuel?
   2. Revision 1 describes low-enriched (LUP) and HALEU (HUP) fuel pebbles. Was a
      startup core of lower-enriched pebbles added or changed after the original
      application? If so, what additional testing and safety analysis does it require, and on
      what schedule?
   3. Please list each research and development item that must be resolved before
      construction is complete, its schedule, and what happens to the construction
      permit if an item cannot be resolved.
   4. Who is the "other company" that will operate the facility? Is there a binding
      agreement today? If operator agreements are deferred to the operating license
      application, what basis did staff use to find the applicant technically qualified?
   5. The NRC's schedule shows the final safety evaluation due in November 2026. Has
      staff already made its technical and financial qualification findings, or will they be
      made in the final safety evaluation? Is any construction permit finding being made
      before the final safety evaluation is complete?
   6. X-energy supplies the safety-related components and fuel but is not the applicant.
      What assurance does the NRC require that X-energy can complete fuel qualification
      and component manufacturing?


7. Additional questions and process requests

Staff committed at the hearing to follow up on at least one question. I ask that the following
receive written answers:

   1. Has the NRC or the Atomic Energy Commission ever denied an operating license for
      a power reactor after granting its construction permit? Please list any instances.
   2. What are the bases for exemptions from the EIS requirement (see the Exemptions
      question in Section 3).
   3. Staff said spent fuel will be stored on site. PSAR Table 2.4.10-1 lists the floor of the
      Spent Fuel Intermediate Storage Facility (SFISF) at 27.4 ft NAVD 88, below the 31 ft
      site grade and about 9 ft below the 36.38 ft design still-water level, the level to
      which flood waters may rise and remain during the design basis flood event (Section
      2.4.10.1). The SFISF, with storage positions for 660 spent fuel canisters, is classified
      NSRST rather than safety-related, so the design basis flood protection requirements
      for safety-related SSCs do not apply to it. The PSAR places its ventilation openings
      at 61.5 ft and analyzes criticality with the storage area flooded (Section 3.10.4). How
      will floodwater be kept out of the SFISF through doors, the Inter-Unit Access Tunnel,
      and walls under hydrostatic pressure? What are the radiological consequences if
      canisters are submerged during a design-basis flood, and for how long could they
      be? The EA (Section 3.14.2.2) concludes that spent fuel storage impacts are not
       significant by relying on the generic Continued Storage GEIS (NUREG-2157), the Fort
      St. Vrain fuel stored in Platteville, Colorado, and German storage experience.
      Where does the EA address flooding of this specific building on the Texas coast, and
      how is sea level rise over the full storage period accounted for?
   4. A resident asked whether an event like the 1991 ethylene oxide explosion at the
      adjacent plant could disable the reactor. Staff answered, at a high level, that it
      would not. Which specific Dow facility hazards (explosions, toxic releases, pipeline
      failures) were evaluated in PSAR Section 2.2, and which were screened out? On
      what basis did staff conclude these hazards pose no undue risk, as 10 CFR
      100.21(e) requires?
   5. A resident described entering a high-security area of the adjacent Dow facility
      undetected in 2002. How will the security plan account for the reactor's location
      within and adjacent to an operating chemical complex?


Additional requests:

   •   Meeting in Seadrift: The facility will be located near Seadrift, and many affected
       residents are commercial fishers who could not attend a 5:00 p.m. meeting in Port
       Lavaca during shrimp season. I request that any future public meeting on this
       facility, including at the operating license stage, be held in Seadrift at a time that
       accommodates working fishers.
   •   Official transcript: Please publish the official hearing transcript in ADAMS and
       identify its accession number in the meeting summary.
   •   Notice: Please add me to the notification list for the meeting summary, any
       supplement to the environmental assessment, and any operating license
       application for this facility.

I appreciate staff's engagement at the hearing and request that each question in this
submission receive a written response in the meeting summary addendum.

Sincerely,

Dan Le
600 Ramona Road
Seadrift, Texas 77983
